Partnership

Unhoused Angelenos get a seat at the table in LA’s charter rewrite

Reach Out LA partnered with Rewrite LA to bring unhoused representation to the 2026 Los Angeles City Charter Civic Assembly, from the first conversations on the street to the assembly itself.

By Reach Out LA · Published March 9, 2026 · Photos by Roman Aytur

Los Angeles is rewriting its city charter, the document that sets out how the city is governed. To give everyday Angelenos a direct voice in that process, the city’s Charter Reform Commission and Rewrite LA convened a civic assembly of residents. Reach Out Los Angeles partnered with Rewrite LA to make sure people experiencing homelessness had a seat at the table.

Listening first

Reach Out volunteers conducted the outreach, meeting unhoused Angelenos where they are and offering them a chance to talk about the problems they face day to day and the solutions they would like to see. Interest in joining the assembly was overwhelming.

Reach Out also facilitated all transportation and stipend distribution, so that cost and travel wouldn’t stand in the way of taking part.

A seat at the table

The 2026 Los Angeles City Charter Civic Assembly met from February 28 to March 8, 2026, bringing together 35 delegates chosen to reflect the city, including residents’ housing status.1 Four of those delegates were unhoused Angelenos.

That is about 11 percent of the assembly. Unhoused residents make up a little over 1 percent of the city: the 2025 homeless count found about 43,700 unhoused people in a city of roughly 3.9 million.2,3 In other words, unhoused Angelenos were represented at roughly ten times their share of the city.

What the assembly recommended

Thirty-one of the 35 delegates supported the assembly’s final recommendations. They include creating a permanent, randomly selected civic assembly that meets at least twice a year, expanding the City Council to 25 districts, and adopting ranked-choice voting.1 The recommendations went to the city’s Charter Reform Commission, and the City Council decides which changes go before voters.

Why it matters

Reach Out began when a group of high school students went to Skid Row to ask unhoused Angelenos what they actually needed. We still believe the people closest to a problem are the most important source of truth. Decisions about how Los Angeles is governed affect unhoused residents as much as anyone, and they deserve a voice in making them.
